finding.claim: Every authorization decision trusts g.user, which this file never sets. If the middleware that sets it takes identity from unverified client input, any caller can impersonate the owner and read, write, or share any note. Unverified precondition, not confirmed.
finding.source: g.user, read at notes.py:28, :35, :44; not set in this file

trace.note: require_view(g.user, n) with g.user from outside this file
can_view compares note['owner'] == user or user in note['shared']

finding.guards_checked: abort(403) checks at notes.py:13, :22, :36 are correct only if g.user is verified identity. No auth middleware is present in this directory.

verdict.guard_found: abort(403) at notes.py:13 (require_view), notes.py:22 (require_edit), and notes.py:36 (write). These abort on failure and are not bypassed, so they are correct for any trusted g.user. Nothing in this directory sets g.user, so no auth middleware is present to check how it is populated.
verdict.reason: The trace matches the code (notes.py:28 → 12 → 8, and 35/44 use the same comparisons), and the abort(403) checks at notes.py:13, :22, and :36 are sound, but whether g.user is verified identity or client-supplied depends on middleware outside this directory that is not present, so exploitability cannot be decided from the code available.

finding.claim: Missing notes return HTTP 500 (KeyError) while existing but forbidden notes return 403, so an authenticated caller can tell which note IDs exist. Impact is limited unless IDs are guessable. Low severity.

trace.note: NOTES[nid] raises KeyError for a missing ID
Existing note the caller cannot view returns 403

finding.guards_checked: Authorization runs after the lookup, so it does not hide existence. No 404 handling exists.

verdict.guard_found: none. notes.py:27, :34 and :43 index NOTES[nid] before any authorization check. The only checks are require_view (notes.py:13) and can_edit/require_edit (notes.py:22, :36, :44), which run after the lookup. The directory contains only notes.py, so no before_request or 404 handler exists anywhere in the codebase.
verdict.reason: notes.py:27 raises KeyError for a missing nid, which Flask turns into a 500, while notes.py:13 returns 403 for an existing note the caller cannot view, so an authenticated caller can distinguish existing from missing IDs. The attacker must be authenticated because g.user is required by notes.py:28, and the existence oracle is real but low severity as claimed.

finding.claim: read() returns the full note including the shared list, so any shared user can see every other collaborator. Low severity, possibly by design.
finding.sink: jsonify(n) returns owner and shared fields (notes.py:29)

trace.note: require_view passes for a shared user
jsonify(n) serializes the whole note, including shared

finding.guards_checked: require_view at notes.py:28 gates access but does not filter response fields.

verdict.guard_found: require_view (notes.py:11-13, via can_view at notes.py:7-8) is the only control. It raises abort(403) on failure, and the call at notes.py:28 is a bare statement that correctly aborts. It gates access only and does not filter response fields, so nothing blocks the shared list from being serialized at notes.py:29.
verdict.reason: The trace holds: notes.py:28 lets a shared user pass require_view (notes.py:7-8, 11-13), and notes.py:29 returns jsonify(n) with the full note, including the shared list. The attacker is a low-privilege user with view access, who cannot otherwise see the collaborator list, so the flaw is reachable. Whether this is a real finding or intended behavior is a product decision; the code itself does not restrict the field.

finding.claim: share() appends an unvalidated owner-supplied value with no type check, dedupe, or existence check, and no endpoint removes access once granted. Business-logic gap, low severity.

trace.note: append of unvalidated value to shared list

finding.guards_checked: Owner-only check at notes.py:44 is correct. No type validation, dedupe, existence check, or revoke path exists.

verdict.guard_found: require_edit (notes.py:20-22, called at notes.py:44) aborts with 403 unless g.user is the note owner. No type validation or dedupe exists, and no revoke route exists, so the owner is the only party who can reach the append.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate (notes.py:44 owner check, notes.py:45 append), but only the note owner can reach the append (notes.py:20-22, 44), and that owner already has full control of the note, so the unvalidated value grants no one new access. What remains is a missing-validation and missing-revoke feature gap, not a vulnerability reachable by an attacker.

finding.claim: No request size limit or list length limit, so a caller can store very large bodies or grow shared without bound by repeated share calls. Low severity, resource exhaustion.
finding.source: Any authorized caller: request.json['body'] (notes.py:37) and request.json['user'] (notes.py:45)

trace.note: body stored without a size check
shared appended on every call with no dedupe or cap

finding.guards_checked: No MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH or length validation appears in this file.

verdict.guard_found: none. No MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH, body length check, or cap on the shared list appears in notes.py. The only controls are require_edit (notes.py:20-22) and can_edit (notes.py:16-17), which restrict the caller to the note owner but do not limit size or count.
verdict.reason: Both trace lines exist and do what the candidate says (notes.py:37 stores request.json["body"] unchecked; notes.py:45 appends request.json["user"] unchecked), so the trace is accurate apart from one wording error: the source is not "any authorized caller" because share (notes.py:44) and write (notes.py:35) both require ownership, so the attacker must be an authenticated note owner, and that owner's unbounded input grows the shared process-wide NOTES dict. The unbounded growth is not blocked by any control in the file, so the finding stands as low-severity resource exhaustion, though the trace's source description should be corrected.
